text.p: These are significant stories in the Nigerian press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Federal government disowns campaigns for military ruler General Sani Abacha to contest next year's presidential poll.
- Commuter train derails near Lagos, one person confirmed dead.
- Curfew lifted in midwestern oil-producing city of Warri where Shell oil company staff were held hostage last month.
- Efforts to end fuel shortage run into a hitch; pumps at Atlas Cove jetty in Lagos are faulty and cannot deliver 16.17 million litres of petrol brought in as a relief measure.

- Hope that Nigerian Telecomms and National Electric Power Authority will be privatised dim as presidency sources say ability of Nigerians to buy such high networth businesses is doubtful and they may end up in foreign hands if sold off.
- Federal Mortgage Bank says will explore the capital market for funds to finance national housing project.
- Nigerian Stock Exchange bars 25 cash-strapped brokers as a computerised clearing system, meant to shorten the time of buying and selling shares, takes off.
- Central bank accounts in Europe and the United States, worth 4.37 billion naira and frozen last year because of the activities of Nigerian fraudsters abroad, have been revived.
- Central bank mops up 141.82 billion naira through sale of treasury bills in the first quarter of this year.

- Nigeria can reap $160 billion from its oil and gas if it increases investment in the industry, says the managing director of Shell oil company in Nigeria, Brian Anderson at a workshop of the Vision 2010 committee in the capital Abuja last week.
- Nigeria Airways settles $4 million part-premium on its insurance and is set to resume international flights.
- A new decree on liquidation of distressed banks is in the works, banking sources say.
